svg.text: The site of failure shapes the motor syndrome
Weakness is shared; tone, reflexes, fractionation, atrophy, sensory and autonomic signs, and time course localize the failure.

B. Central-lesion signs depend on time and lesion type
Schematic clinical courses — not patient data
Spasticity is a possible later component of a central motor syndrome—not its immediate definition and not an inevitable outcome.
C. ALS can affect both upper and lower motor systems
Profiles vary across patients and over disease.
Weakness is the shared symptom; tone, reflexes, fractionation, atrophy, sensory and autonomic signs, and time course reveal where the motor system failed.
